newsitem.title: FRENCH POLYNESIA: Tahiti plans to double post-atomic tourism, pearls.
newsitem.headline: Tahiti plans to double post-atomic tourism, pearls.

text.p: French Polynesia plans to double pearl production and income from tourism by the year 2005 to make up for a cash shortfall after France ended nuclear testing in the South Pacific, officials said on Wednesday.

Paris has pledged to pay French Polynesia 990 million francs ($190 million) a year until 2005 to make up for the lost military investments after the final series of six atomic tests beneath the Mururoa and Fangataufa atolls that ended in January.

Looking to a post-nuclear age, French Polynesia's social, economic and cultural council has approved a plan to double production of farmed pearls, including Tahiti's celebrated black pearls, by the year 2005.
The plan would raise sales of pearls to 1.1 billion francs ($210 million) in the year 2005 from 550 million ($105 million) in 1995, the officials said.

The council, meeting on Monday, also approved a plan to double revenues from tourism to 2.75 billion francs ($530 million) by 2005 from about 1.4 billion ($270 million) in 1995, partly by creating 3,000 extra hotel beds.
The plan would mean attracting 300,000 to 320,000 tourists a year, up from fewer than 200,000 in 1995 to the islands' palm-fringed beaches and azure waters.

The Territorial Assembly, representing the islands' 210,000 inhabitants, will examine the plan before local president Gaston Flosse presents it to French authorities. Polynesia is a French overseas territory with a large degree of internal autonomy.
The French military are currently tearing down military and scientific buildings on Mururoa under a plan to return the atoll to its pre-atomic state as a tropical paradise.
